payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Turn the image into a drawing made from chalk
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does chalk-like mark-making render both giraffes and the substantial surrounding scene?
node.criteria: Pass if chalk-like contours, powdery or broken strokes, layered strokes, or rubbed chalk shading visibly describe both giraffes and substantial surrounding regions. These are alternative manifestations of chalk, not features that must all occur everywhere. Broad rubbed shading can qualify when its direction, boundaries, layering or pigment variation describes depicted forms; uniform grain or loss of sharpness alone cannot. Inspect the giraffes separately from the vegetation, hills, sky and ground: convincing marks in one region cannot substitute for chalk rendering in the other. Fail if either the giraffes or substantial surrounding regions are rendered only by photographic detail, generic grain, blur or smearing without form-describing chalk marks. Color, smooth blended passages, recognizable anatomy and retained composition are permitted. Return unknown only if visual evidence is unavailable or genuinely insufficient; transport or schema failures are not visual failures.
node.binding: Compare the supplied SOURCE and EDITED images for the requested transformation into a drawing made from chalk. Inspect the contours, spots and shading of both giraffes, then inspect vegetation, hills, sky and ground for form-describing chalk strokes or rubbed shading rather than merely changed texture.

node_traces.evidence: Both giraffes have visibly drawn, dark outlined contours and patterned spots with layered, broken-looking strokes and shaded areas. The surrounding vegetation, hills, sky, and ground also show directional, rubbed strokes and tonal variation that describe the scene's forms, rather than only uniform grain or blur.

Both giraffes have visibly drawn, textured contours and layered shading that describe their anatomy and spots. The surrounding vegetation, hills, sky, and ground also show directional, rubbed strokes and tonal variation that follow the scene's forms, rather than only uniform grain or blur.

Both giraffes are described with visibly drawn, broken chalk-like contours and layered, powdery shading, including their spots and limbs. The surrounding vegetation, hills, sky, and ground also show broad directional rubbed strokes and tonal variation that describe the scene rather than merely adding uniform grain. The composition remains recognizable.

Both giraffes retain recognizable contours and spots, but their shading and edges appear mostly smoothed or blurred rather than described by clear chalk-like strokes or rubbed, layered marks. The surrounding vegetation, hills, sky, and ground are heavily smeared into broad directional blur; this changes texture but does not visibly describe those forms with chalk mark-making.

Both giraffes have visibly drawn, chalk-like outlines and textured, layered shading across their bodies and spots. The surrounding vegetation, hills, sky, and ground also show broad directional strokes and rubbed shading that describe the scene’s forms, rather than only uniform grain or blur.

d1_drawn_representation: The node’s binding already captures the key regions, but its broad “represented by drawn marks” test appears to over-credit a stylized finish. The traces repeatedly cite outlines, spots, broad strokes, and chalk-like grain, then infer that the whole scene is drawn; they do not separately test whether substantial regions still retain photographic structure. In the edited image, the giraffes and nearby vegetation show clear drawn treatment, while the hills, sky, and ground are largely smeared into broad tonal fields, with source composition and some photographic modeling still apparent. Refine the decision criterion to assess each region independently and distinguish constructed marks/forms from blur, smudging, or texture alone; require evidence that substantial environmental areas have actually been re-expressed, not merely softened. Keep the whole-image completion judgment separate from evidence of partial progress, so strong animal treatment cannot automatically make the entire transformation a pass. The repeated high-confidence “yes” traces despite the partial reference suggest a systematic criterion/binding gap, not a transport or dependency failure; do not treat repetition or confidence as proof of completion.
